title: CEO Interview with Lisa Spelman of Cornelis
gist: Cornelis CEO Lisa Spelman (ex-Intel Xeon head) argues the network is the last passive layer in AI/HPC infrastructure, and that congestion and latency leave expensive accelerators idle. Cornelis designs its own SuperNICs and switches and is on its third-generation platform, with 50+ OEM/ODM design wins and 500+ datacenter deployments. It just announced an Active Compute Fabric with programmable RISC-V cores at every hop, built on UALink/ESUN for scale-up and Ultra Ethernet for scale-out, and pitched as vendor-neutral.

themes.theme: Network as the bottleneck for AI economics

insights.claim: Cornelis CEO Lisa Spelman argues that compute, storage and memory have all become workload-aware, while the network is the last passive layer. As compute speeds up, the largest training, inference and simulation jobs spend more time waiting on data, leaving expensive compute idle.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: As accelerator spending grows, more of the value at the margin moves to networking that raises utilization, which supports AI networking silicon vendors.
insights.quote: The network is the last passive layer.
insights.locator: Over the last decade, compute, storage, and memory

insights.claim: Cornelis argues that AI and HPC jobs send bursts of small messages across thousands of endpoints and often cannot advance until all of them arrive. Conventional networks that drop and retransmit packets under congestion therefore force the whole job to run at the speed of its slowest exchange.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Tail latency, not peak bandwidth, sets cluster throughput, which favors fabrics with lossless, congestion-managed designs.
insights.quote: forcing the job to run at the speed of its slowest exchange
insights.locator: In the network, that challenge shows up

insights.claim: Cornelis manages congestion proactively with credit-based flow control, telemetry-driven adaptive routing and per-packet path selection, aiming to maximize productive compute per watt and per dollar.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Performance per watt is the selling metric, so power-constrained AI buildouts are where Cornelis would be most competitive.
insights.locator: We designed our network to manage congestion

insights.claim: Spelman says many organizations still plan the network last, size it by bandwidth and treat it as a byte carrier. At AI factory scale, she argues, buying accelerators first and fixing the network later yields clusters that look impressive on paper but underdeliver in production.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: If buyers move to co-designing compute and network, network vendors capture a larger share of AI capex and gain more say in procurement.
insights.quote: Buying accelerators first and solving the network later produces a cluster that looks impressive on paper and underdelivers in production.
insights.locator: Many still plan the network last

themes.theme: Active Compute Fabric with RISC-V in-network compute

insights.claim: Cornelis announced the Active Compute Fabric, which puts programmable RISC-V cores at every hop across every NIC and switch. The cores accelerate collectives, KV cache and mixture-of-experts routing while accelerators keep doing math, and customers can tune them instead of relying on fixed-function in-network processing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Programmable in-network compute is a new way to compete with fixed-function offload from InfiniBand and Ethernet incumbents, and it gives RISC-V another foothold in datacenter infrastructure.
insights.quote: adds programmable RISC-V cores at every hop, across every NIC and switch
insights.locator: We start from a different assumption

insights.claim: Cornelis frames the competitive landscape this way: InfiniBand and Ethernet keep getting faster but were built only to move data between endpoints, and DPUs and SmartNICs added intelligence and offload at the edge. In its view the fabric in between stayed passive, and in-network processing is usually fixed-function.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Cornelis is positioning against both the InfiniBand and Ethernet camps on architecture rather than raw speed, a claim that needs benchmark evidence before it can be credited.
insights.locator: We differentiate in how we think

insights.claim: Cornelis builds its fabric on open standards, with UALink and ESUN for scale-up and Ultra Ethernet for scale-out. It supports mixed CPUs, GPUs and accelerators so customers are not tied to a single compute vendor's roadmap.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Cornelis benefits if open scale-up standards gain ground against proprietary single-vendor stacks, so track UALink and Ultra Ethernet adoption as its tailwind.

insights.claim: Spelman says mixed CPUs, GPUs and workload-specialized accelerators are becoming the norm, so operators need interoperable networks that do not lock them into one vendor's architecture.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous clusters reduce the pull of bundled compute-plus-network offerings and open the market to independent fabric vendors.

insights.claim: Cornelis is moving into scale-up networking. Spelman argues that new compute challengers are designing at the rack level rather than the chip, and that open scale-up gives them a path to complete rack-scale systems without adopting a single vendor's stack. In her words, every scale-up domain eventually becomes a scale-out problem.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Rack-scale challengers to the dominant GPU vendor are a natural customer base for open scale-up fabrics, so watch for design wins with them.
insights.quote: Every scale-up domain eventually becomes a scale-out problem, which is why we’re building for both.
insights.locator: I’m particularly excited about our move into scale-up

insights.claim: Cornelis is working on the third generation of its networking platform. It reports more than 50 OEM and ODM design wins and deployments in over 500 datacenters, including new large-scale installs at Lawrence Livermore National Lab and the Texas Advanced Computing Center.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Its traction is anchored in national-lab HPC. The open question for investors is whether it converts to commercial AI cluster wins.
insights.locator: We’re working on the third generation

insights.claim: Cornelis sees its strongest fit in communication-intensive work: large-scale AI training, disaggregated inference, mixture-of-experts models and distributed inference pipelines. On the HPC side, it lists scientific computing, engineering simulation, weather and climate modeling, and national research environments.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: MoE and disaggregated inference are growing workloads where network latency matters more, which widens the market for latency-optimized fabrics.
insights.locator: On the AI side, that includes

insights.claim: Most Cornelis customers buy through OEM partners, and its technology is qualified across a broad range of systems from major OEMs worldwide. Customers are encouraged to benchmark their own applications on the fabric before committing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: OEM-led distribution lowers sales cost and adoption friction but makes Cornelis dependent on OEM prioritization against InfiniBand and Ethernet alternatives.
insights.locator: Most customers engage with us through our OEM partners

insights.claim: Cornelis CEO Lisa Spelman previously led Intel's Xeon Products and Solutions business as Corporate Vice President in the Data Center & AI Group.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Leadership with deep datacenter go-to-market experience at Intel strengthens Cornelis's OEM relationships and its credibility with buyers.
